title: Release candidate 2 on paper, batch 4: pages 14 to 19, chapter 3, Everything is connected: graphs, and the start of chapter 4, Where do you land?
how: Six photographs of pages 14 to 19 of the printed candidate; notes 84 to 143, continuing the series. The handwriting was read by the journalist; four readings are uncertain and marked so.

first-page.name: The first pages sell the book
first-page.principle: The opening is about the reader, and the reason to read comes first (Zoom in, not discover).

show.name: Show the book, do not list it
show.principle: A story or a picture where an argument would do less.

altitude.name: Topics first, details under them
altitude.principle: Detail the point does not need is cut (Zoom in, not discover).

process-out.name: The making-of out of the reader's way
process-out.principle: The 2018 book and its outlines go to the section at the end.

voice.name: The voice is mine
voice.principle: Lines that sound odd, hedged or not like Dinis are rewritten.

reader-context.name: Meet the reader where they are
reader-context.principle: Explain a term before using it, with a short analogy, and say it first, then link.

evidence.name: Fact or opinion, visibly
evidence.principle: The reader can see which claims are backed by data and which are Dinis's opinion, and the data is found (Follow the rabbit holes).

links.name: The website holds what the page cannot
links.principle: Where the book needs more room, a QR code sends the reader to the site: the source, the explainer, the visualisation.

works.name: What works, keep it
works.principle: The ticks: what the pen approves is kept, and the format it likes is used again.

answers.name: Answers to For Dinis
answers.principle: Where the candidate asked Dinis a question in a For Dinis box, the pen answers it, and the next candidate acts on the answer.

visual.name: Draw it
visual.principle: Where an idea is a shape (a graph, a map, an evolution, a comparison), the book draws it instead of describing it.

doing.name: Doing starts early, and runs through
doing.principle: A manual, not a journey: you learn by doing, so you start doing early (Zoom in, not discover).

notes.written: Basically here we really need to make the (visual) case of "why graphs" & why they are so powerful & why they are everywhere
notes.means: Chapter 3 has one job: show, visually, why graphs, why they are so powerful and why they are everywhere.

notes.written: it's not their fault, the industry terminology is all over the place [left: Reword, too harsh]
notes.means: 'I have met people for whom a graph is a picture with boxes' blames the reader; the industry's words are the problem. Reword.

notes.written: give more analogies of what is a node & an edge
notes.means: More analogies for a node and an edge, before the definition.

notes.written: not relevant at this stage of the book
notes.means: The graphs book on graphs.sgit.ai is not for page 14.

notes.written: meaningless is too strong [and] each edge is a signal
notes.means: 'A node connected to nothing is literally meaningless' overstates it; say instead that each edge is a signal.

notes.written: needs rewrite
notes.means: The three things people mean by graph needs rewriting.

notes.written: my use of graph [...] this is wrong ↓ a graph node can be anything ↓ since a chart is a graph too ↓ see the "thinking in graphs" or "fractal semantic graphs"
notes.means: 'Never a chart, never a figure' is wrong: a node can be anything, and a chart is a graph too. Take the definition from thinking in graphs, or fractal semantic graphs. (The first words are partly uncertain.)

notes.written: [struck with a wave: In 2018 I left an outline for a chapter called Graphs ...] see →
notes.means: Cut the 2018 outline.

notes.written: see graphs.sgit.ai
notes.means: The answer to For Dinis: the presentation on graphs is graphs.sgit.ai.

notes.written: DEMEANING [circled: easier]
notes.means: That a Generation Z reader will find the chapter easier than Dinis's generation did is demeaning.

notes.written: these kind of references are weird since the reader has not read them [beside: In Follow the rabbit holes]
notes.means: Do not cite a chapter the reader has not reached as if they had read it.

notes.means: Fractal semantic graphs is the idea that can shift the reader's thinking: focus the chapter on it and explain it.

notes.written: [struck: The newsroom's introduction to what I call]

notes.written: this is a good way to start explaining graphs → connections
notes.means: 'The world is made of connections; groups of groups are how we think' is a good way into graphs.

notes.means: 'A chain that ends in a rumour is a finding too' needs a better word than finding.

notes.written: define better [circled: A refactor is]
notes.means: Define refactor better, for a reader who has not met the word.

notes.written: rewrite [the newsroom example struck]

notes.written: this needs to be a common theme across the book [beside: It does not matter where you start; it matters that you start.]

notes.means: Every page, or section, could carry a QR code to itself online, at its version, and the visits would drive revenue.
